t: Data portability, file formats and compression
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L05: Data portability, file formats and compression.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Define data portability and explain why standard file formats support it. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Data portability means being able to move data from one computer, device or application to another without having to type it in again. Mark schemes also accept the words interoperability or compatibility. Portability depends on file formats. A file format is the agreed way that data is laid out inside a file, and the file extension, such as dot jpg or dot csv, shows which format is used. If data is saved in a standard format, many different programs on many different systems can open it.
Makes sense. Keep going.

For example, a youth football club in Lisburn might keep its members in a database, export them as a csv file and send that file to the league, which opens it in a spreadsheet. Nothing is retyped, so time is saved and no new errors are introduced. Choosing the right format matters. If you pick a format that the other person cannot open, or one that loses quality or formatting, the data is not truly portable.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Jpeg is the usual format for photographs. It uses lossy compression, and the user can choose how much, so files are small and load quickly on web pages. Png uses lossless compression, keeps every detail and supports transparent backgrounds, which makes it good for logos. Gif can only use 256 colours, but it is lossless and can store a series of images that play one after another as a simple animation. Tiff keeps very high quality and moves easily between Windows and Apple computers, so it is used for printing and scanning, but files are large.
Got it. Keep going.

Pict is Apple's own graphics format and can hold bitmap and vector images. For text, txt holds plain text with no formatting at all. Csv stores table data with commas between the fields. Rtf keeps basic formatting such as fonts and bold and can be opened by most word processors. Pdf, created by Adobe, keeps fonts, images and layout exactly the same on every device, and is usually read-only.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Wav stores sound without any compression, so the quality is high but the files are large, which makes it suitable for recording and editing. Mp3 compresses sound using lossy compression. It removes sounds that most people would not hear, giving a much smaller file that still sounds close to the original, so it is used for music and podcasts. Wma is Microsoft's compressed audio format, made for Windows Media Player. Midi is different from all the others.
Okay. Keep going.

It does not store recorded sound at all. Instead it stores instructions such as which notes to play, on which instrument and for how long, so the files are tiny and can be passed between electronic keyboards and computers. For video, mp4 compresses both the pictures and the sound and can also hold subtitles and still images; it is widely used for streaming. Mpeg is named after the group of experts who created standards for compressing video. Avi is a Microsoft format that keeps audio and video in sync, but files are often large.
Go on.

Compression reduces the size of a file. Smaller files take up less storage space and can be uploaded, downloaded and emailed more quickly, which is important for web pages, streaming and attachments with size limits. There are two types. Lossy compression permanently removes some of the data, such as fine detail or colours that people are unlikely to notice. Files become much smaller, but some quality is lost and the original can never be fully recovered.
Right. Keep going.

Jpeg, mp3 and mp4 use lossy compression, and it suits photos, music and video. Lossless compression makes the file smaller without throwing any data away, so when the file is decompressed it is exactly the same as the original. Zipping a folder with a program such as WinZip is lossless, and so is png. Lossless compression does not shrink files as much, but it must be used for text documents, spreadsheets and programs, because losing even a small part would change the data or stop it working.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Data portability?
Being able to move data between computers, devices or software applications without typing it in again, usually by saving it in a standard file format.
File format?
The standard way data is organised inside a file, shown by its file extension (e dot g..jpg,.csv), which determines which programs can open it.
Compression?
Reducing the size of a file so it needs less storage and can be uploaded or downloaded more quickly.
Lossy compression?
Compression that reduces file size by permanently removing some data, so some quality is lost and the original cannot be fully restored, e dot g. jpeg, mp3.
Lossless compression?
Compression that reduces file size without losing any data, so the file can be restored exactly as it was, e dot g. zip, png.
CSV?
Comma-separated values: a text format in which each line is a record and the fields are separated by commas; used to move table data between spreadsheets and databases.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

File formats appear almost every year. Multiple-choice questions on image and video formats came up in the 2019 paper, question 1 to (c), and the 2021 paper, question 10 and the 2025 paper, question 3 asked for formats and their uses. the 2022 paper, question 11 asked about portability and compared jpeg with tiff: credit came from saying jpeg uses lossy compression and gives small files for the web, while tiff keeps high quality for printing but makes large files. the 2021 paper, question 2 tested exporting database data to csv. The Chief Examiner reported that portability was poorly answered, so learn a precise definition: moving data between computers or applications without re-entering it. For compression, give a reason such as faster upload or less storage, and when comparing lossy and lossless always state that lossy loses data permanently while lossless can be restored exactly. When asked to choose a format, name it and justify it with a feature that fits the task.
Let's finish with a question for the listeners. Which audio format stores musical instructions rather than recorded sound? Is it A, wav; B, mp3; C, wma; D, midi?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is D: midi. Midi stores which notes to play, on which instrument and for how long.
